new_statements.quote: Sandía and Isleta: i, u, e as in Taos; a as in Picurís; ə higher than in Taos (high-back unrounded); ie, ia as in Taos; əa, ua as Taos əo, uo; nasal vowels correspondingly. ... In all four languages the vowels are long with loud (main) or medial (secondary) stress, on all three tones, and short and somewhat obscured when weak-stressed ("unstressed"). The loud and medial stresses occur with three tones: normal tone, marked with a raised straight stroke before the vowel for loud stress, and a lowered stroke for medial stress ... low tone ... high tone ... The normal-toned stresses are much like ordinary English main and secondary stresses, high tone has a decidedly higher pitch, and low is much lower and with a drawling of the vowel.
new_statements.citation: Trager, George L. 1943. The kinship and status terms of the Tiwa languages. American Anthropologist 45(4): 557-571.
new_statements.locator: p. 559 (phonological introduction covering Taos, Picuris, Sandia and Isleta); Isleta and Sandia term lists pp. 566-567
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: copies we hold (lines 4766-4782) and the page image American Anthropologist 45(4), p. 559) carry the quoted passage verbatim; the ellipses in the reader's quote only omit the sentence on nasal ə̨ and the notation examples ('a, ˌa; low tone à; high tone á; 'for the low and high, medial stress need not be separately marked, as of two lows or two highs the first is loud..'). The scanned garbles a few symbols (ə as 'a', Sandía as 'Sandia') but the page image matches the quote exactly. Surrounding section read (pp. 557-559, 566-567, leaf62-64, 71-72): Trager states the orthography is phonemic and uniform for Taos, Picuris, Sandia, Isleta; the prosodic paragraph is explicitly 'In all four languag…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Trager (first-hand fieldwork at Isleta 1935/1937-38 and Sandia) analyses Southern Tiwa, like Taos and Picuris, as having three degrees of stress (loud, medial, weak) cross-cut by three tones (normal, high, low) on loud- and medial-stressed syllables; stress is written lexically on each word and no rule for its position is given. His Isleta forms show loud stress on different syllables in different words (e.g. p|ap'ade 'older sibling' with loud stress on the second syllable vs. m'atu?ude 'relative', c'unu 'nephew' with loud stress on the first; ?əw'ade ~ ?'əw- recorded with two stress placements), i.e. stress is treated as contrastive/unpredictable within a tonal system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A 'medial (secondary)' stress degree is posited and marked; Trager notes that when a high or low tone co-occurs with a normal-toned stress in a word, relative loudness is predictable (of two lows or two highs the first is loud; of a high and a low the high is loud).
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; one Isleta item (A'. ?əw'ade) explicitly recorded with an alternative 'normal stress' placement ?'əw-.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern citation forms of nouns (singular absolute, plural, stem); the description is a joint statement for all four Tiwa languages, with Isleta and Sandia data from Trager's own fieldwork. Later first-hand description (Leap 1970:73, not seen) reportedly keeps the same three-stress/three-tone analysis; Sutton 2014:429 regards Southern Tiwa tone/prosody as essentially undescribed.
new_statements.identity_note: Trager 1943 treats 'Sandia' and 'Isleta' as two closely similar languages and gives one joint prosodic statement for all four Tiwa varieties; his Southern Tiwa data are first-hand from Isleta Pueblo (1935/1937-38, rechecked 1957-59) and one Sandia speaker. Both are dialects of Glottolog sout2961 Southern Tiwa (Isleta incl. Ysleta del Sur, and Sandia). Leap 1970 (not seen) describes Isleta only; Brandt 1970 (not seen) Sandia only.
